title: Episode 306: Edward IV: The Sun in Splendour, Elizabeth Woodville, and the Restoration

The turbulent, glamorous life of King Edward IV, the first Yorkist monarch of England. Standing six-foot-four with striking good looks and ferocious battlefield prowess, Edward seized the crown at just eighteen years of age after the bloody victory at Towton. His secret, scandalous love match with the widowed Lancastrian commoner Elizabeth Woodville alienated his chief ally, Warwick the Kingmaker, igniting renewed civil war that drove Edward into exile. Returning with unmatched audacity in 1471, Edward crushed his enemies at Barnet and Tewkesbury to reclaim his throne. Discover the hedonistic yet invincible king who won the English crown twice.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series chronicles the first king of the House of York: an invincible battlefield commander whose secret marriage shook a kingdom, who lost his crown only to win it back in blood and mist: King Edward IV. Here is George with the extraordinary story of the Sun in Splendour.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE VISION OF THE THREE SUNS: MORTIMER'S CROSS: FEBRUARY 1461
In February 1461, eighteen-year-old Edward, Earl of March, stood in the frostbitten fields of Herefordshire near Mortimer's Cross, facing a powerful Welsh Lancastrian army led by Jasper Tudor and Owen Tudor. Edward was reeling from the horrific news of the Battle of Wakefield, where his father Richard, Duke of York, and his younger brother Edmund had been slaughtered, their severed heads mocked with paper crowns above the gates of York. As dawn broke across the cold Welsh border, an astonishing meteorological phenomenon appeared in the winter sky: three distinct, dazzling suns, a parhelion or sun dog caused by ice crystals in the upper atmosphere. Terrified soldiers crossed themselves and fell to their knees, fearing a divine omen of impending doom. But young Edward, towering six-foot-four in gleaming plate armor, stepped forward before his trembling ranks. With booming confidence, he pointed his broadsword to the heavens, declaring that the three suns represented the Holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost—or the three surviving sons of the House of York, signaling God's unmistakable favor for their cause. Edward ordered his men to charge. His forces swept the Lancastrians from the field, executing Owen Tudor at Hereford, and Edward adopted the 'Sun in Splendour' as his personal and immortal royal badge. Weeks later, following the apocalyptic blizzard of Towton where twenty-eight thousand men fell, Edward marched into London to be crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey. Owen Tudor, the grandfather of future king Henry VII, was led to the execution block in Hereford marketplace, unable to believe he was about to die until the collar was ripped from his neck. As the executioner raised his broadax, Tudor murmured that his head would lie on the same block where it was wont to lie upon Queen Catherine's lap. Edward's victory at Mortimer's Cross firmly established his martial credentials across the kingdom, proving that despite his youth, he possessed the cold, unhesitating resolve necessary to avenge his fallen father and claim the English throne.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SECRET MARRIAGE: ELIZABETH WOODVILLE: MAY 1464
Edward was young, athletic, charismatic, and adored by the ladies of London. But while his chief kingmaker and cousin, Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was in Paris negotiating a prestigious diplomatic marriage for the king with Princess Bona of Savoy, sister-in-law to the French king, Edward was harboring an explosive secret. In May 1464, while hunting near Stony Stratford, the twenty-two-year-old king was captivated by Elizabeth Woodville, a radiant, golden-haired widow five years his senior, whose late husband Sir John Grey had died fighting for the Lancastrians at St. Albans. Elizabeth, clutching her two small sons beneath the Oak of Honor, petitioned the king for the return of her confiscated dower lands. Edward, smitten by her beauty, attempted to make her his mistress, but Elizabeth placed a dagger to her breast, declaring that while she was too humble to be his queen, she was too proud to be his concubine. Awed by her virtue, Edward married her in absolute secrecy in an early morning ceremony at her family manor in Grafton Regis, with only the priest, a clerk, and the bride's mother Jacquetta of Luxembourg present. When Edward finally revealed the marriage to a stunned Royal Council at Reading Abbey in September 1464, Warwick was mortified and furious: England's monarch had spurned European royal royalty to marry an impoverished Lancastrian commoner whose grasping relatives soon monopolized the finest marriages and titles in the realm. The elevation of the Woodville family sparked unprecedented jealousy among the established Anglo-Norman aristocracy. Elizabeth's father, Sir Richard Woodville, was created Earl Rivers and Lord High Treasurer, while her twenty-year-old brother John Woodville was scandalously married to the wealthy Katherine Neville, Dowager Duchess of Norfolk—a woman in her late sixties, an arrangement contemporaries decried as a 'diabolical marriage'. Warwick watched his diplomatic alliances shattered and his influence eclipsed by a grasping clan of court parvenus, planting the seeds of deadly aristocratic rebellion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE KINGMAKER'S TREASON AND THE FLIGHT TO FLANDERS: 1469 TO 1470
Warwick's simmering resentment toward the rising Woodville clan soon boiled over into treason. Seducing Edward's jealous, fickle younger brother, George, Duke of Clarence, with the promise of the crown and marriage to his daughter Isabel Neville, Warwick orchestrated armed rebellions across the north. In 1469, after Yorkist royalists were routed at Edgecote Moor, Warwick seized King Edward and held him prisoner at Middleham Castle. But the Kingmaker discovered that governing without an anointed king was impossible; lawlessness exploded, and Warwick was forced to release Edward. Undeterred, Warwick fled to France, where King Louis XI brokered an unthinkable alliance between Warwick and his mortal enemy, the exiled Queen Margaret of Anjou. Warwick's daughter Anne was betrothed to Margaret's son, Prince Edward, and in September 1470, Warwick invaded England with French gold. Caught completely unprepared in Yorkshire as his own northern commanders defected, King Edward was forced to flee for his life. Galloping to the port of King's Lynn with a handful of loyal companions, including his faithful younger brother Richard, Duke of Gloucester, Edward boarded small Dutch merchant ships, escaping to Flanders with only the clothes on his back, leaving his pregnant queen Elizabeth Woodville to flee into sanctuary at Westminster Abbey, where she gave birth to his heir, Prince Edward. During his captivity at Middleham, Edward maintained a facade of serene unconcern, hunting deer in the Yorkshire forests and affably banqueting with his guards, confident that the realm could not function without him. When lawlessness broke out and Warwick found he could not raise a single commission of array without the king's signature, Edward gently reminded the Kingmaker that an anointed English monarch could never be governed by a subject. Warwick's desperate alliance with Margaret of Anjou in Angers required the proud Earl to kneel on cold stone before the French queen for fifteen uninterrupted minutes in silent penance before she deigned to speak to him.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE RETURN AT RAVENSPUR AND RECONCILIATION WITH CLARENCE: MARCH 1471
In Flanders, protected by his wealthy brother-in-law Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, Edward plotted his resurrection. Securing fifteen hundred Flemish mercenaries and fifty thousand gold florins, Edward sailed for England in March 1471. In an eerie echo of Henry Bolingbroke seventy-two years earlier, Edward landed at Ravenspur on the Yorkshire coast. When hostile northern towns closed their gates, Edward employed Bolingbroke's identical deception: he donned an ostrich feather in his cap, crying 'King Henry!' and claiming he returned solely to claim his rightful inheritance as Duke of York, not the crown. As he marched southward through the Midlands, thousands of Yorkist retainers flocked to his banner. Near Banbury, a momentous encounter occurred: Edward's treasonous brother Clarence, realizing that Warwick intended to restore the Lancastrian dynasty rather than make him king, rode out with four thousand men. In full view of both armies, the two brothers dismounted, embraced each other with tears, and Clarence begged for royal forgiveness. Edward gladly welcomed his brother back into the Yorkist fold. Marching directly into London without resistance, Edward was acclaimed by the citizens, freed the frail Henry VI from the Tower, and retrieved his wife and newborn son from sanctuary. As Edward's small fleet sailed from Flanders, a tempest scattered his ships across the North Sea, leaving him to land at Ravenspur with barely five hundred men. When the Recorder of the city of York barred the city gates against him, Edward placed a sprig of broom—the planta genista—in his bonnet, swearing on the holy sacrament that he sought only his paternal duchy. His reconciliation with Clarence near Banbury was a masterstroke of psychological manipulation: Edward had secretly sent Clarence's sisters to remind him that Warwick viewed him only as an expendable pawn, playing upon George's vanity to detach four thousand seasoned men from the rebel cause.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FOG OF BARNET AND THE SLAUGHTER OF TEWKESBURY: APRIL TO MAY 1471
Edward's crowning military masterpieces came in rapid succession in the spring of 1471. On Easter Sunday, April 14, Edward met Warwick at the Battle of Barnet just north of London. A thick, impenetrable blanket of early morning spring fog covered the battlefield. In the blinding mist, the battle lines overlapped: Warwick's right wing routed the Yorkist left, but when the victorious Lancastrian soldiers under the Earl of Oxford returned through the fog to the center, their badge of a 'Star with Rays' was mistaken by their own comrades for Edward's 'Sun in Splendour'. Thinking they were being attacked by Yorkists, Warwick's center unleashed friendly fire upon Oxford's men, who shouted 'Treason!' and fled in panic. In the ensuing rout, Warwick the Kingmaker was hunted down in a nearby wood, struck from his horse, and slain through his open visor. Three weeks later, after a punishing march of forty miles in a single day under a scorching sun, Edward intercepted Queen Margaret's Lancastrian army at Tewkesbury on May 4. Edward's artillery and cavalry charges shattered the Lancastrians, trapping them against the River Severn. Lancastrian Prince Edward of Westminster was cut down fleeing the field, and the captured Lancastrian lords were beheaded in the marketplace. That night in London, the frail Henry VI was murdered in the Tower. The House of York was supreme. The carnage in the blinding fog of Barnet was described by Sir John Paston as an inferno of mist and steel, where men hacked blindly at phantoms in the gloom. Warwick's brother, John Neville, Marquess of Montagu, was slain in the center, and when the Kingmaker fled toward his warhorse tied in the woods, Yorkist knights surrounded him, dragged him down, and drove daggers through his throat. At Tewkesbury, the young Lancastrian Prince Edward of Westminster was butchered in cold blood after the battle, with some chroniclers claiming Clarence and Gloucester struck him down in King Edward's presence after the boy offered an insolent reply to the monarch.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BUTT OF MALMSEY: THE EXECUTION OF CLARENCE: 1478
With his domestic enemies annihilated, Edward enjoyed twelve years of unparalleled security, establishing an efficient, solvent monarchy by enforcing customs revenues and extracting an enormous annual pension of fifty thousand crowns from King Louis XI of France in the Treaty of Picquigny in 1475. Yet domestic peace was poisoned by the incurable treachery of his brother George, Duke of Clarence. Following the death of his wife Isabel, Clarence spread malicious slanders that Edward was an illegitimate bastard fathered by an archer named Blaybourne, and accused Queen Elizabeth of witchcraft. When Clarence was implicated in necromancy and treasonous plots against the king's life, Edward's patience finally snapped. In January 1478, the king personally prosecuted his brother for high treason before Parliament in Westminster Hall. Clarence was condemned to death. To avoid the public spectacle of a royal duke being beheaded on Tower Hill, Clarence was executed privately inside the Tower of London on February 18, 1478. According to persistent and widely accepted contemporary accounts, Clarence—known for his excessive fondness for sweet fortified wine—was drowned in a massive butt of Malmsey wine. Though Edward had eliminated his treacherous brother, the execution cast a dark, lingering shadow over the royal family and weighed heavily on the king's conscience. Clarence's downward spiral was accelerated by grief, alcohol, and paranoia after his wife Isabel died in childbed. Convinced she had been poisoned by her servant Ankarette Twynyho, Clarence seized the poor woman, dragged her to Warwick, and forced a jury to convict and hang her within three hours, a blatant perversion of the King's common law. At Clarence's parliamentary trial, Edward stood before the Lords and personally recited his brother's endless acts of treason, perjury, and rebellion, weeping with fury as he demanded the death penalty against his own flesh and blood.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TWILIGHT OF THE KING: PROSPERITY AND UNTIMELY DEATH: 1483
In his final years, Edward transformed from a vigorous, athletic warrior into an indulgent, corpulent epicurean who spent royal revenues on magnificent palaces, Italian silks, illuminated manuscripts, and lavish feasts. He patronized William Caxton, who set up England's first printing press at Westminster in 1476. Edward indulged in notorious womanizing, openly keeping three celebrated mistresses whom he described as the merriest, the wiliest, and the holiest harlot in the realm—the merriest being the witty and beautiful London goldsmith's wife, Jane Shore. But years of gluttony, heavy drinking, and luxurious living wrecked his iron health. In April 1483, after catching a violent fever during a fishing trip on the River Thames, forty-year-old King Edward IV collapsed and took to his deathbed at Westminster Palace. Sensing his end, the dying monarch attempted to reconcile the bitter factions at his court, commanding the Woodville family and Lord Hastings to clasp hands and swear eternal friendship. He appointed his fiercely loyal younger brother, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, as Lord Protector of his twelve-year-old heir, Edward V. On April 9, 1483, Edward IV died at the age of forty. He was buried in St. George's Chapel at Windsor Castle, leaving behind an unstable realm on the brink of an unforeseen dynastic catastrophe. Despite his legendary sensuality, Edward was an administrator of remarkable financial acumen: he personally engaged in international wool and cloth trade using royal merchant vessels, dramatically reduced royal household waste, and died as the first English king since Henry II to leave a solvent treasury unencumbered by debt. His magnificent Great Hall at Eltham Palace, with its soaring hammerbeam roof, stood as a monument to his architectural patronage. Yet by failing to secure the minority of his young son or rein in the bitter feud between the Woodvilles and the old nobility, Edward left the realm on the precipice of ruin.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. If you enjoyed this chapter of Edward IV: The Sun in Splendour, Elizabeth Woodville, and the Restoration, subscribe to the show, share it with a fellow history lover, and tune in next Tuesday for our next journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
